HEADLINE: Young and hungry to get to the top in 2020
TEXT:
Private equity Meet Australia's top 20 dealmakers under 40

The hardest thing in private equity land is putting money to work.

There's $11 billion sitting on the sidelines in Australia looking for a home - and plenty of managers offshore who also have an eye out for an Australian deal. And while the private equity firm founders and the old guard still hold the keys to the war chests, increasingly they're relying on the new wave of dealmakers to unearth fresh ideas and turbocharge portfolio companies.

It's a big opportunity for 30-something dealmakers trying to make a name for themselves. The veterans know it's a people game and they're competing with each other for the next star fund manager, banker or lawyer.

For the up and comers, the best way to put their name up in lights is to strike a big deal or two. Get that right and there are promotions, invitations to firm partnerships and/or opportunities to cut the ties and go it alone, all of which spell big paydays and the chance to outdo long-time rivals.

While it's tough for the rising stars to find new assets at affordable prices, the good news is that the exit window is open for existing investments.

Bigger private equity firms are happy to snap up existing portfolio companies - think Craveable Brands, likely Archer Capital's illion and Next Capital's Funlab - while trade buyers are paying up for synergies where they see an opportunity. The initial public offering route is challenging, but bankers will still talk it up as viable.

Among the firms, the crack squad at KKR, led by David Lang, had a huge 2019, buying MYOB and Arnott's, while Quadrant Private Equity, BGH Capital and Pacific Equity Partners lead the next level of deals down. Newcomer Jefferies had a big year advising buy-side clients, while Goldman Sachs had success selling assets to private equity.

So here's a list of 20 private equity young guns to watch in 2020, in no specific order. Each is younger than 40 and in a battle to join the top echelon of Australian dealmakers.

Alex Eady

Eady has hit the big time at Quadrant Private Equity. He has worked with firm founder and Australian buyout industry legend Chris Hadley for close to a decade and is credited with investments including Zip Industries and Canberra Data Centres, both of which saw Quadrant partner with founders and make about 3.5 times its money in double-quick time. Next year he is expected to steer a potential exit of the firm's human services business APM, which makes about $500 million a year revenue. He is renowned for his ability to win company founders' and management teams' trust. Internally at Quadrant he is regarded as similar to former under-40s listee Jonathon Pearce, who neatly executed a take-private of QMS Media at the end of the year.

Kelly Morton

Morton's expertise is in helping private equity firms line up debt for new and existing portfolio companies. She has done the bulge bracket investment banking scene, and worked for one of the big four Aussies, and is running her own shop Skye Capital Advisory. Morton was on this list last year - and backed it up with another busy period. This year she helped mid-market firm Adamantem Capital buy ASX-listed Legend Corporation and Allegro Funds' bet on struggling retailers formerly owned by Steinhoff Asia Pacific. She also oversaw refinancings for listed corporates such as Costa Group and Domain. Clients are known to respect her no-nonsense approach and integrity.

Beau Dixon

Dixon is an investment director at Sydney-based Anchorage Capital Partners and another returnee. He is known for his origination, disciplined negotiation and diligence skills and - perhaps most importantly - has been able to deliver returns for investors. Dixon played a role in the acquisition, turnaround and sale of mining services group Contract Resources, which limited partners said returned about three times their money in only two years. He also originated and executed the firm's $200 million-odd acquisition of rolling-stock leasing and maintenance business CF Asia Pacific, which is due to complete early in the new year. Dixon is seen as a potential future leader in the firm along with fellow investment director Todd Twining.

Andrew Charlier

Charlier is hitting his straps as a managing director at Pacific Equity Partners. Like well-regarded colleague Evan Hattersley, he hails from Bain & Company's consultancy business - the tried and tested route at PEP - and has been with the firm since 2007. Charlier now sits across PEP's secure assets and buyout funds giving him access to two of the biggest pots of capital in domestic private equity. Charlier helped PEP buy the Asia-Pacific arm of trailer and towing parts company Horizon Global in a competitive auction, and has been heavily involved in raising funds for the Secure Asset Fund which is expected to close at $500 million next year. He also signed off on PEP's first few secure assets deals including smart meters business Intellihub. His rise confirms that PEP has the deepest bench of active dealmakers in the local market, spearheaded by the likes of Tony Duthie, and former listees David Brown and Shannon Wolfers who this month pitched a $1 billion bid at Village Roadshow.

Alex Elser

Elser gets straight to the point. While plenty of lawyers want to run clients through a long list of risks, the King & Wood Mallesons partner is known for cutting straight to the big ones and handling the others herself. She has her clients' trust and is regarded as a strong deal executor and negotiator, honing her skills with the help of veteran lawyer Mark McNamara since 2010. Elser's had a busy year working on OPTrust's Kinetic, the stub equity in Affinity Equity Partners' Scottish Pacific, the rollover equity in Healthscope's buyout, and Affinity's sale of its stake in Velocity Frequent Flyer.

Paul Griffiths

US investment bank Jefferies has burst on to Australia's financial sponsors' scene. Its dealmakers are hungry and have head office's blessing to underwrite debt deals to help clients fund new acquisitions. Paul Griffiths heads local financial sponsors coverage. The ex-BofA banker works closely with Jefferies Australia boss Michael Stock, who is well known in the private equity sector, and together they have been pitching hard and winning work. Jefferies was sole adviser to KKR on its $3.2 billion acquisition of Arnott's and is working to sell Affinity's MedicalDirector.

David Brooks

Brooks has run quarterback for two of BGH Capital's first three acquisitions. The former TPG Capital rising star, and long-time right-hand man to firm founders Ben Gray and Simon Harle, helped BGH secure cyber security roll-up CyberCX, which involved the acquisition of 12 underlying businesses, and New Zealand-listed dental company Abano Healthcare under the guidance of Harle and fellow BGH founder Robin Bishop, respectively. Brooks, a BGH partner, is regarded for his strong deal execution skills and ability to bring along the next generation of dealmakers including Steve Scordilis and Oliver Bowler. He is a key part of the team that oversees the country's biggest buyout fund.

Srdjan Dangubic

While the big end of private equity hogs the headlines, its smaller end often has more success getting deals done. Sydney's Five V Capital had a huge year, raising a new fund and quickly signing three deals. Srdjan Dangubic is the young gun in the team, working alongside ex-CVC dealmaker Adrian Mackenzie. Dangubic is well regarded as experienced - having worked in Australia and overseas - professional and down to earth.

Will Broughton

Goldman Sachs has repeatedly found itself the investment bank selling to private equity. And while managing directors Tim Freeman and Zac Fletcher head its coverage, much of the heavy lifting is done by the next level down. One name that comes up repeatedly is Will Broughton - a consumer banker who happens to be married to gun UBS banker Jessica Curtis. Consumer has long been a busy hunting ground for private equity in Australia. Broughton is currently selling RM Williams for L Catterton and Laureate Education's local arm, and was involved in defending Navitas from BGH Capital, selling Arnott's to KKR and in PAG's acquisition of Craveable Brands. Also keep an eye on Andrew Chong at Goldies and the pair Broughton & Co butt heads with the most in PE land: Morgan Stanley's Luke Boeg and UBS' Nick Alexander.

Crystal Russell

Russell would have better insights into the Australian private equity scene than most. She spearheads QIC's Asia Pacific fund and oversees co-investment opportunities for the $80 billion-odd asset manager. Russell helped establish QIC's secondary market coverage and process - which has led to a number of acquisitions and divestments - and is a member of its global private capital leadership team and investment committee. She also focuses on investment strategy for the Asia Pacific, which includes QIC's commitment to the likes of cancer care provider Icon Group.

Rob Hooke

While Melbourne's Advent Partners was founded in 1984 and is one of the country's oldest private equity firms, its partners are mostly in their 30s and 40s. It is a quiet achiever of the local private equity scene, having been able to deal with all-important succession planning to be cashed up and looking to invest in 2020. Rob Hooke is one of the firm's partners alongside Brad Lynch, Symon Vegter and Mark Jago. He is yet to hit 40 and has been a driving force behind some strong deals in recent years. Hooke was involved in Compass Education and Tribe Breweries and was instrumental on the way in for Junior Adventures Group (and the subsequent sale of a majority stake to Quadrant) and Frosty Boy.

Noah Obradovic

Obradovic is in Tom Story's private equity team at law firm Allens. The managing associate joined Allens from UK firm Freshfields where he spent three years in its crack private equity practice. Obradovic is said to be very commercial and regarded for his ability to understand private equity clients' objectives, which puts him on the same wavelength as the senior dealmakers paying his bills. In the past year alone he advised KKR on its acquisition of Arnott's and BGH Capital on its failed bid for Healthscope. He also worked for Pacific Equity Partners on its purchase of Horizon Global's local arm, and Cerberus, which acquired Axsesstoday.

Gareth Woodbridge

Woodbridge is on a fast track at KKR. He had a huge 2019 - leading its charge for Arnott's in conjunction with Australian private equity team head David Lang and preparing pubs group Australian Venue Co for an exit next year - and was rewarded with promotion to managing director at the firm in December. He also spearheads KKR's investments in Laser Clinics Australia and GenesisCare - which this month paid $1.5 billion to acquire Florida-based 21st Century Oncology - and is known to be close to KKR head office in New York, which is both necessary and powerful for someone in the Australian outpost of one of the world's biggest buyout investors. Woodbridge works for David Lang in a team that also includes fellow up-and-comers Boris Dangubic and Rupert Pedler.

Chris Allen

Allen is another returnee. The MinterEllison partner works closely with Riccardo Casali and is known for his attention to detail, willingness to be always available for clients and ruthless pursuit of a transaction. He is gaining a reputation as a go-to legal adviser among Australia's private equity shops, seeking to follow in the footsteps of KWM's Mark McNamara, Allens' Tom Story, Gilbert + Tobin veteran Peter Cook and Freehills' Damien Hazard. Allen's got a gig on Affinity's mooted MedicalDirector exit, and advised Allegro Funds on its acquisition of WA's biggest radiology business Perth Radiological Clinics this year, Mercury Capital's late-stage talks to buy Bauer Media's local magazines arm and VGI Partners' various raisings and listing.

David Slocomb

Slocomb is back investing with his former boss at The Carlyle Group, Simon Moore, after a few years as an operations specialist at fast food chain Guzman Y Gomez - tidying it up nicely ahead of the TDM Investment - and later Oaktree Capital Management. We are told to expect big things of the Colinton Capital junior partner in 2020, including bedding down his first acquisition for his new employer.

Oliver Tompkins

Oliver Tompkins, 36, is one of four partners at Mercury Capital working alongside one of the sharpest minds in the sector, ex-Goldman Sachs investor Clark Perkins. Tompkins is said to be measured and quiet in his approach, yet has had considerable success picking sectors and companies that prove to be winners. He's heavily involved with Mercury's Message Media and Squiz, which are out of its $600m Fund III and also Fiftyfive5 which is from Fund II. His strength is working on founder relationships.

Mark Chudek

At the Brett Sutton-led regional buyout giant Affinity Equity Partners, which has had a huge year in terms of exits, there is a young gun coming through the ranks that he has been keeping under wraps. Mark Chudek, an Affinity vice president, was heavily involved in Affinity's investment in Velocity Frequent Flyer (sold back to Virgin Australia this year) and at its next big sale, medical practices software company MedicalDirector. Chudek has worked closely with Sutton and fellow managing director Rami de Marchi, but is starting to carve out a name for himself thanks to the way he is regarded by management teams and founders, and his collaborative approach.

Vincent Wong

'Vinnie' Wong is the young gun leading TPG Capital's investment charge in Australia. Boss Joel Thickins is known for delegating deal leadership to his troops. Wong helped stitch up the firm's acquisition this year of Greencross - where senior adviser Rob Speedie is working his magic - as well as Novotech last year, and helped manage its stakes in Ingham's and Healthscope in the past few years. He is multi-lingual and leads TPG's healthcare sector responsibility, which is a keen area of focus for Thickins, his right-hand man Speedie and the big bosses offshore. While Wong's name was mentioned in a few places, others pointed to younger TPG dealmaker Michael Frawley as one to watch. Meanwhile, Thickins has also drafted Dan Lahav from Allen and Co in New York to start in mid-January as a vice president.

David and Craig Tozer

Tozer and Co, an advisory and investment firm set up by twin brothers Craig and David Tozer, is a newcomer to Australian financial markets but is one to watch. The firm had a breakout deal when it helped global giant The Carlyle Group into ASX listed Pioneer Credit, and has been in and around a handful of other special situations. While the Tozers are a left-field choice for this list, recent history shows they have ideas, relationships and can execute on transactions.

Alastair Corrigal

Law firm Gilbert + Tobin has cemented its place in the minds of big private equity investors, thanks in part to the tireless efforts of leading duo Peter Cook and Rachael Bassil. But a handful of other G+T lawyers are winning plenty of work, including Melbourne's Alex Kauye who is close to KKR, TPG and the investment banks, and Alastair Corrigal. Corrigal in particular is tipped for a strong 2020. He has built a reputation working for The Carlyle Group and CPE Capital (formerly CHAMP Private Equity), advising CPE when it sold Accolade Wines to Carlyle and helping Carlyle exit Coates Hire. More recently, he helped CPE into Marand Precision Engineering and the Banksmeadow waste processing facility.

HEADLINE: Impressive Boxing Day crowds fail to boost faith in retail
TEXT:
Retail sales growth over the Christmas trading period will languish at levels last seen during the global financial crisis for the foreseeable future, industry figures predict.

Australian Retailer Association boss Russell Zimmerman admitted yesterday he was uncertain consumers would spend the $2.5 billion he had forecast for Boxing Day, typically the highlight of the shopping calendar.

He said wasn't entirely confident they would "hit those big numbers", citing several headwinds like bushfires and late November discounts.

"There is a whole raft of changes in retail that we're grappling with as we move forward."

Sydney's Pitt St Mall was buzzing with bargain hunters on Boxing Day, but some shoppers expressed ambivalence.

Andrew Barnes, 24, exemplified the challenge for retailers. The Brisbane photographer who is visiting Sydney with his parents for Christmas, said his decision to come to the sales was unplanned.

"It was just more about hanging out with family," Mr Barnes said. "Which, I guess, always gives you a few spending ideas along the way."

At 10am he was holding a large bag containing a $250 blender from JB HiFi. However, , although he acknowledged it was an excellent opportunity to buy, he didn't plan to keep spending.

"If you're going to buy something, you might as well get it when it is 20-30 per cent off. Otherwise, I'd just get it online," he said.

Mr Zimmerman was heartened by the Boxing Day crowds and his meetings with retailers, but he estimated that Boxing Day spending would increase only 2.3 per cent on last year's figure, while the ARA's projection for the pre-Christmas period - November 14 to Christmas Eve - showed was just 2.6 per cent higher than last year.

"Not since the GFC have we forecasted such slow growth. Retailers usually expect a three in front of that number," Mr Zimmerman said, pointing to last year's forecast for the pre-Christmas of 3.7 per cent growth.

"I believe this is the new normal. I don't think retailers should be expecting the increases that they are used to any more."

Mr Zimmerman blameda combination of disruptions, like the rise of online shopping and "Black Friday" sales in late November that lured spending out of the traditional period.

Environmental factors, such as the drought gripping eastern Australia and rampant bushfires across the country, also took their toll on spending habits, he said.

Overall, the ARA - in consultation with the Roy Morgan Research Institute - put pre-Christmas spending at $52.7 billion this year.

Although Mr Zimmerman thought the prediction was on the mark due to a "large bang late in the piece", no one will know for sure what the figure is until the Bureau of Statistics reveals its retail trade figures in February.

Someone who came to the sales with the intention of spending was Genaro Reyes from Stanhope Gardens in Sydney's west. The 51-year-old stepped out with wife Maryann, 50, and their three daughters for family time.

Although he does most of his shopping online, each of his daughters had about $200 to play with at the sales.

"It's not really about shopping," Mr Reyes said. "We're just following the kids; we've giving them what they want."

The National Retail Association, a rival retail lobby to the ARA, is more optimistic. Its chief Dominique Lamb said Boxing Day remained the pinnacle of Australian retail, and she believed the crowds were a good sign for the NRA's spending projection of $2.6 billion.

The crowds had been impressive, Ms Lamb said from Brisbane. "There are people out and about looking for deals."

Her organisation came to its figure - a 5.2 per cent increase on 2018 - by working with Queensland University of Technology researchers and was confident a bumper Boxing Day would put retail back on track.

She conceded that smaller operations might be at risk due to a slower than expected lead-up period but said larger operators were a different story as they were better equipped t to deal with the changing nature of retail, especially when considering their adjacent online and physical storefronts.

"We know those online figures are the growth point for retail," Ms Lamb said. "The best thing for us is that most of our brick-and-mortar stores have online stores too."

Still, she believed the physical experience of shopping would keep brick-and-mortar operations alive in the future.

Retailers need more Boxing Day shoppers like Ben and Diane Touma, who enjoyed the physical experience of shopping and spent freely.

The mid-40s couple from Fairfield in Sydney's west said they had splurged about $2000 yesterday morning and had plans for more.

"Every year we do a Boxing Day shop," said Mr Touma, who was carrying four shopping bags. "You work hard; you deserve it."
